items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-16
items.q: The interviewee (Nick La Rocca) is responding to an interviewer's letter that lists Bunk Johnson among other musicians who left New Orleans. La Rocca does not mention Bunk Johnson in his rebuttal, nor does he claim any personal interaction, collaboration, or specific knowledge of him beyond the gene

ctx.x: Pioneer of jazz wins recognition, New Orleans, editor from New Orleans States. It was gratifying to read in your paper on February 27th the article on Nick LaRocca, famous leader of the original Dixieland jazz band. He deserves the honor accorded him and his band by the Jazz Club of England whose leader, Marcus O'Donoghau visited our sea last summer. If Mr. LaRocca accepts this invitation, and I hope he does, I'm sure he will mention some of the other bands that played jazz at that time. Tom Brown, who took his…

I'd like to comment on the dates that she has here to show you she was eaten up, taken in by this communist propaganda. I wish you'd hear this tape recorder. Buddy Bolin, Freddie Kepler, George Pequet left here in 1911. In 1906, by the things that I have in my hand, from Louisiana State Mental Hospital at Jackson, Louisiana, Bolin was incarcerated in there in 1906. He couldn't have played with them. And I've told you when these Negroes came it was 1917. Clarence Williams, he says, left here around 1911 or 13.…

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-09
items.q: No, I never... I don't know who this man is, but this is before my time.

ctx.x: There's an answer there to this, WDSU. Alright, this is WDSU channel 6, I'm sorry, WDSU TV channel 6, New Orleans, WDSU Broadcasting Corporation, 520 Royal Street, New Orleans 16, Louisiana, Tulane 4371. January 4th, 1957, Mr. Nick LaRocca, 2218 Cousin Street, New Orleans 13, Louisiana. Dear Nick, our manager, Mr. Robert Swayze has passed to me your letter of January 13th relative to a program on jazz music which we carried in the summer of 1935. I have made a rather thorough search for the script of this program…

Almond Hug with regards with regards with what has been said. Arm and Hug being a young man, I didn't think it was the right thing for me to do to contact this boy because this program was put on by the WDSU programming department. And all this was all mapped out and planned before they went on the air what was to say. Furthermore, if you took the Dixieland Licks away from Arm and Hug, he wouldn't even play piano because that's all he plays, Dixieland Licks, to embellish his music with. There's a man probably 40…
No, I never... I don't know who this man is, but this is before my time.

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1959-06-14
items.q: I've heard some of the recreations, some of these records of Bunk Johnson and people like that who were relying on their memories of what they played.

ctx.x: And they're saying there was some part of the creation of jazz. That Jack Lane, who played a drum and lousy drums at that, created jazz. Now that's good enough for men who thrive on thievery, on a word that we had nothing to do. Our jazz was started in Chicago. We took in the ragtime and changed the rhythm in Chicago. In 1916, we seen we were going to be a flop the first night. And I, being a good dancer, I watched those people. At that time, they had Vernon Castle doing the castle walk. And everybody was trying…

No, I wrote that mostly as a sort of, you might say, editor. Walter Allen managed to interview the various musicians that were still living. And he sent me the facts and I wrote them, sewed them up together. I was more concerned with the records than with the legends. I wasn't very interested in these obscure people from the shadows who were said to have played with this, that and the other musician, in this, that and the other band, and who never made any records at all. I'm not interested in music I can't hear…

Now, they say that this, but Freddie Kepit, they make a great big story about it, that he was asked by the Victor Company to record. He says he didn't want to record because he didn't want the world to know his stuff. But they didn't know that I knew all this stuff. They thought that I was just a dumb man, that I didn't know what was going on. They imported them all. The Kepits, the Olivers, and all of them, they all died in the gutter. None of them made good. None of them could make a record. They had to steal…
